scope: Right-angle branching paths and impersonal advice across all twelve expansion pages

changes.before: A garden gives you choices that a shopping list does not. You can try a different variety, pick young leaves for lunch or grow something that rarely appears in the shops. I grow artichokes partly because I like them and partly because I can seldom buy them locally. Their value to me is greater than their weight in a basket.
changes.after: A garden gives you choices that a shopping list does not. You can try a different variety, pick young leaves for lunch or grow something that rarely appears in the shops. If you like artichokes but seldom find them locally, they can be worth growing. Their value to you may be greater than their weight in a basket.

changes.before: Where the site allows, I run long beds north to south so tall crops share their shade across the day. Existing buildings and drainage may matter more than compass neatness. Watch where rain collects before settling the layout.
changes.after: Where the site allows, run long beds north to south so tall crops share their shade across the day. Existing buildings and drainage may matter more than compass neatness. Watch where rain collects before settling the layout.

changes.before: Mounded beds need no timber and leave fewer crevices for slugs in my wet garden. Framed beds hold a flatter surface and can raise the working height. Choose what makes the plot easier to use, then prepare the ground using the Cultivation pages.
changes.after: Mounded beds need no timber and leave fewer crevices for slugs in a wet garden. Framed beds hold a flatter surface and can raise the working height. Choose what makes the plot easier to use, then prepare the ground using the Cultivation pages.

changes.before: Allow for mature plants, working space, an open door and roof vents. I quickly outgrew my small greenhouse. A larger second-hand frame may cost surprisingly little, but check that it is sound and complete, and allow for dismantling, transport and replacement glass. Photograph joints before taking it apart.
changes.after: Allow for mature plants, working space, an open door and roof vents. A small greenhouse can soon become crowded. A larger second-hand frame may cost surprisingly little, but check that it is sound and complete, and allow for dismantling, transport and replacement glass. Photograph joints before taking it apart.

changes.before: I use soil beds in my greenhouses because they give roots room to grow and hold a reserve of moisture. They also save a considerable procession of pots and bags of potting compost.
changes.after: Soil beds in a greenhouse give roots room to grow and hold a reserve of moisture. They also save a considerable procession of pots and bags of potting compost.

changes.before: On soil, leave the growing areas open to the ground below. Loosen construction-compacted soil before filling with topsoil and mature compost, or build a no-dig surface over suitable ground. My brick-edged beds sit above the outside soil level for drainage; the raised greenhouse frame preserves height for tall plants. Plan a clear doorway at the same time.
changes.after: On soil, leave the growing areas open to the ground below. Loosen construction-compacted soil before filling with topsoil and mature compost, or build a no-dig surface over suitable ground. Brick-edged beds can sit above the outside soil level for drainage; a raised greenhouse frame preserves height for tall plants. Plan a clear doorway at the same time.

changes.before: You do not have to build internal brick walls. My smaller greenhouse has mounded growing areas with a woodchip path between them. On a paved site, use suitable containers instead. Whatever the arrangement, check root moisture regularly; a soil bed gives you a buffer, not permission to forget the watering.
changes.after: You do not have to build internal brick walls. A smaller greenhouse can have mounded growing areas with a woodchip path between them. On a paved site, use suitable containers instead. Whatever the arrangement, check root moisture regularly; a soil bed gives you a buffer, not permission to forget the watering.

changes.before: Early salads can occupy space before the summer crops need it. In my greenhouse, the spinach comes out as it begins to crowd the tomatoes; after summer, suitable autumn salads can follow. Use the crop guides for timing. Open doors and vents in warm weather, shade when needed, and clean the glass and service moving parts before the new season.
changes.after: Early salads can occupy space before the summer crops need it. Remove spinach as it begins to crowd the tomatoes; after summer, suitable autumn salads can follow. Use the crop guides for timing. Open doors and vents in warm weather, shade when needed, and clean the glass and service moving parts before the new season.

changes.before: I use a flexible core rotation, rather than four equal blocks. Small beds let me grow more of what we eat. Keep permanent crops, such as asparagus, outside the annual shuffle. Move kitchen onions each year, as their crop guide advises.
changes.after: A flexible core rotation need not use four equal blocks. Small beds let you grow more of what your household eats. Keep permanent crops, such as asparagus, outside the annual shuffle. Move kitchen onions each year, as their crop guide advises.

changes.before: Why I now use three
changes.after: Why three bins help

changes.before: I began with two bins, but found myself bagging up finished compost to make room. Three lets each job have its own space. You do not have to shovel the contents along a row: the bins change jobs as they become empty. With only two, finish using one before you need to start filling it again.
changes.after: With two bins, you may need to bag up finished compost to make room. Three bins let each job have its own space. You do not have to shovel the contents along a row: the bins change jobs as they become empty. With only two, finish using one before you need to start filling it again.

changes.before: Secure a suitable metal rodent barrier across the base and its edges, while allowing drainage and soil life access. Check joints, lids and damaged boards regularly. My own long-term version uses brick walls.
changes.after: Secure a suitable metal rodent barrier across the base and its edges, while allowing drainage and soil life access. Check joints, lids and damaged boards regularly. Brick walls are an option for a permanent version.

changes.before: Dampen dry cardboard and other dry additions as they go in. Close the lid to keep heavy rain out and moisture in, then check below the fresh top layer during dry weather. In my enclosed bins I do not routinely turn the contents. If yours stalls, check for dry corners or wet clumps; break these up, adding water to dry material or dry browns to a soggy mix.
changes.after: Dampen dry cardboard and other dry additions as they go in. Close the lid to keep heavy rain out and moisture in, then check below the fresh top layer during dry weather. In these enclosed bins, there is no need for routine turning. If yours stalls, check for dry corners or wet clumps; break these up, adding water to dry material or dry browns to a soggy mix.

changes.before: Finished compost is dark, crumbly and earthy, with little recognisable soft plant material. Pick out remaining coarse stalks and return them to the filling bin. Give slow material more time. My resting bin may spend many months getting ready; the plants will not thank you for impatience.
changes.after: Finished compost is dark, crumbly and earthy, with little recognisable soft plant material. Pick out remaining coarse stalks and return them to the filling bin. Give slow material more time. A resting bin may spend many months getting ready; the plants will not thank you for impatience.

changes.before: Spread mature compost on no-dig beds, or incorporate it when preparing a dug bed. Keep it clear of established soft stems. For potting on, I sieve equal volumes of good mature compost and garden topsoil and mix them thoroughly. Try a small batch first: the ingredients vary from garden to garden.
changes.after: Spread mature compost on no-dig beds, or incorporate it when preparing a dug bed. Keep it clear of established soft stems. For potting on, sieve equal volumes of good mature compost and garden topsoil and mix them thoroughly. Try a small batch first: the ingredients vary from garden to garden.

changes.before: For me, organic growing begins with a useful bit of housekeeping: keep as much plant material as possible in the garden, turn it into compost and return it to the soil. Then pay attention to what grows well there.
changes.after: Organic growing begins with a useful bit of housekeeping: keep as much plant material as possible in the garden, turn it into compost and return it to the soil. Then pay attention to what grows well there.

changes.before: I once copied a thick hay-and-straw mulch that worked well in drier climates. On my cold, wet ground it became a home for slugs. That taught me to try new ideas on a manageable area before changing the whole garden. Keep what works, understand why it works, and feel free to adapt it.
changes.after: A thick hay-and-straw mulch that works well in a drier climate can shelter slugs on cold, wet ground. Try new ideas on a manageable area before changing the whole garden. Keep what works, understand why it works, and feel free to adapt it.

changes.before: Collect rainwater from suitable roofs into covered butts on firm, stable stands. Keep the supply close enough to use easily. Soil beds hold more reserve than small pots, but check both in hot weather. In my heatwave garden, newly planted brassicas struggled despite daily watering; delaying planting and providing temporary shade would have helped more than another soaking.
changes.after: Collect rainwater from suitable roofs into covered butts on firm, stable stands. Keep the supply close enough to use easily. Soil beds hold more reserve than small pots, but check both in hot weather. Newly planted brassicas can struggle in a heatwave despite daily watering; delaying planting and providing temporary shade may help more than another soaking.

changes.before: Prepare a fine, firm surface and remove competing weeds. Make a drill at the depth given for the crop; water it first if dry. Sow, cover and firm gently, then keep the seed zone moist. On coarse no-dig compost, I use a little sieved compost in the drill and over the seed.
changes.after: Prepare a fine, firm surface and remove competing weeds. Make a drill at the depth given for the crop; water it first if dry. Sow, cover and firm gently, then keep the seed zone moist. On coarse no-dig compost, use a little sieved compost in the drill and over the seed.

changes.before: Modules give early crops a start while outside soil is still cold. Sow at the crop’s depth, label with variety and date, and give the seedlings light and steady moisture. I favour modules early in the year; later, a small outdoor nursery bed is often easier than nursing young outdoor crops through a hot greenhouse.
changes.after: Modules give early crops a start while outside soil is still cold. Sow at the crop’s depth, label with variety and date, and give the seedlings light and steady moisture. Use modules early in the year; later, a small outdoor nursery bed is often easier than nursing young outdoor crops through a hot greenhouse.

changes.before: For an odd corner, I sometimes broadcast mixed salad seed. Choose crops with compatible sowing times, covering depths and picking sizes. Scatter evenly, cover as required and water gently. Thin before the strongest swamp the rest, and keep a separate main sowing of any crop you are relying on.
changes.after: For an odd corner, try broadcasting mixed salad seed. Choose crops with compatible sowing times, covering depths and picking sizes. Scatter evenly, cover as required and water gently. Thin before the strongest swamp the rest, and keep a separate main sowing of any crop you are relying on.

changes.before: Two rectangular garden layouts: finger paths enter from one edge; leaf-vein paths branch from a central spine inside a rectangular bed. Both leave growing soil beyond the path ends.
changes.after: Two rectangular garden layouts: finger paths enter from one edge; evenly spaced paths branch at right angles from a central spine inside a rectangular bed. Both leave growing soil beyond the path ends.

exceptions: Source titles remain verbatim; inclusive our ancestors / our bodies in John’s supplied seasonal paragraph is not autobiographical and is retained. Frozen approved references remain intact. The approved Why Grow baseline is preserved, with the requested impersonal amendment in the working copy.
